name: Bass guitar
subtitle: Be the heartbeat
description: Lock in the pulse, connect the chords, and give every song its foundation.
tuning: Four-string standard tuning, thickest to thinnest: E1 A1 D2 G2. Bass notation sounds one octave lower than written.

lessons.title: One note, a whole groove
lessons.goal: Play four relaxed open E notes and mute the space between them.
steps: Support the bass with a strap, sitting or standing. Keep the neck slightly raised and both wrists comfortable. Tune E1 A1 D2 G2, thickest to thinnest.
Rest your picking thumb on the pickup or a lower string. Pull your index fingertip gently across the thick E string, rather than snapping it away from the instrument.
At 60 BPM play four E1 notes, one per beat. Stop each note just before the next with your picking hand.
Repeat with the middle finger. Aim for equal volume and a clear pulse, not speed. Turn the amplifier down before plugging in or unplugging.
lessons.tip: E1 is about 41 Hz. Phone microphones may struggle with it; try the 12th fret E2, or use on-screen practice and self-assessment.
lessons.assessment: I played four even low E notes and controlled the ringing.

quiz.question: The bass's thickest open string in standard tuning is...
quiz.explanation: A four-string bass is E1 A1 D2 G2, from thickest to thinnest.

lessons.title: Two fingers, one pulse
lessons.goal: Alternate index and middle fingers with consistent tone.
steps: Play open A1 with index, middle, index, middle. Let the plucking finger land gently on the adjacent lower string.
At 50 BPM play eight notes, one per beat. Listen for equal volume between fingers.
Move to D2 and repeat. Rest the thumb on the A string to mute it, while another part of the hand controls the E string.
Play A1 four times, then D2 four times. Stop if your hand tenses and rebuild the motion slowly.
lessons.tip: Muting is a musical skill: unused strings should stay quiet, even when your fretting hand is moving.
lessons.assessment: I alternated both plucking fingers and kept unused strings quiet.

quiz.question: What does muting do?
quiz.explanation: Both hands help stop strings you are not intentionally playing.

lessons.title: Find the notes on the neck
lessons.goal: Read bass tab and play E-F-G without squeezing.
steps: On the thick E string, fret 1 is F1 and fret 3 is G1. Place the fingertip just behind the wire, not on top of it.
Use index for fret 1 and little finger for fret 3 if that is comfortable. Shift the hand slightly rather than forcing a wide stretch.
Read E|0-1-3-1-0| and play one note per beat at 45 BPM. The number is the fret; 0 is open.
Use minimal pressure. A buzzing note often means your fingertip should move closer to the fret wire, not press harder.
lessons.tip: Bass frets are wide. Smaller hands can shift; a forced one-finger-per-fret stretch is not required in low positions.
lessons.assessment: I read the tab and played the five notes with a relaxed fretting hand.

quiz.question: Moving one fret higher raises pitch by...
quiz.explanation: Each fret is one semitone; twelve frets make an octave.

lessons.title: Follow the root
lessons.goal: Support a C-F-G-C progression with bass roots.
steps: Find C2 on the A string fret 3, F1 on the E string fret 1, and G1 on the E string fret 3.
Play C for four beats, F for four, G for four, and C for four. A root is the note a chord is named after.
Start with one note per bar; next try four quarter notes per bar. Use 50 BPM and mute when changing strings.
Try the original C-F-G-C backing in the studio. Listen for the moment the chord changes, then place your root on beat 1.
lessons.tip: The root is enough. Supporting the chord and time is more important than adding extra notes.
lessons.assessment: I followed C-F-G-C and landed each root on beat 1.

quiz.question: The root of an F major chord is...
quiz.explanation: The root gives the chord its letter name: F for F major.

lessons.title: Checkpoint: steady ground
lessons.goal: Play an original root-note groove for eight bars.
steps: Use C2 F1 G1 C2, one bar each, repeated twice. Set the metronome to 55 BPM.
Play the root on beats 1 and 3, holding each for nearly two beats. Count 1-2-3-4 without rushing.
Mute before the next bar and change to its root. Repeat the eight bars twice without stopping.
Pass when you can keep the pulse, make clean string changes, and keep unplayed strings quiet. Use a teacher or your own listening for rhythm feedback.
lessons.tip: The reference demonstrates pitches, not the two-beat holds. Use the written counts to shape the groove.
lessons.pattern: C C | F F | G G | C C · each note lasts 2 beats · repeat
lessons.assessment: I played Steady Ground twice with clean muting and steady time.

quiz.question: What is the most important first job of this bass line?
options: Play as many notes as possible
Support the harmony and steady pulse
quiz.explanation: A simple bass line with strong time makes the whole group feel secure.

lessons.title: Build a major scale
lessons.goal: Play one octave of C major and locate its half steps.
steps: Find C2-D2-E2-F2-G2-A2-B2-C3 using A-string frets 3,5,7; D-string frets 3,5,7; G-string frets 4,5. Shift the whole hand rather than over-stretch.
At 40 BPM play ascending, one note per beat, alternating index and middle plucking fingers.
Reverse the pattern. Mute strings as you leave them and make every note equal in volume.
Listen for the half steps E-F and B-C. Hum the scale, then find a different fingering for one note using the fretboard.
lessons.tip: This shifting route avoids forcing a wide low-position stretch. The fretboard shows frets 0-7; every note in this route is available.
lessons.assessment: I played the scale both ways with clean shifts and even plucking.

quiz.question: C major's half steps are...
quiz.explanation: A major scale follows whole-whole-half-whole-whole-whole-half steps.

lessons.title: Root, fifth, octave
lessons.goal: Create a bass line from stable chord tones.
steps: For C, use C2 (A3), G2 (D5) and C3 (G5). For F use F1 (E1), C2 (A3) and F2 (D3). For G use G1 (E3), D2 (A5) and G2 (D5).
Play root-fifth-octave-fifth, one note per beat at 45 BPM. Keep the higher octave light rather than accenting it accidentally.
Connect one bar of C, one F, one G, and one C. Listen for the root on every beat 1.
Try the C-F-G-C backing. If the string crossings blur, return to two-note root-fifth patterns before adding the octave.
lessons.tip: A perfect fifth is seven semitones above the root; an octave is twelve.
lessons.pattern: Each bar: root fifth octave fifth · C F G C
lessons.assessment: I connected root-fifth-octave patterns with clean string changes.

quiz.question: The perfect fifth above C is...
quiz.explanation: C-D-E-F-G spans five letter names and seven semitones.

lessons.title: The space between beats
lessons.goal: Play an eighth-note pickup without rushing the next beat.
steps: Count 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & at 50 BPM. Clap 1, 3 and the '&' after 4.
On C2 play a quarter note on 1, a quarter note on 3, then a short eighth note on 4&. Remain silent on the unplayed counts.
Repeat four bars. The note on 4& leads into the next beat 1, but must not make beat 1 arrive early.
Apply the same rhythm to C-F-G-C. Use controlled note lengths and mute during rests; try 60 BPM only when all gaps are deliberate.
lessons.tip: The metronome gives numbered quarter beats. Supply the equal '&' subdivisions yourself.
lessons.pattern: Per bar: root on 1,3,4& · silence elsewhere · C F G C
lessons.assessment: I placed the 4& pickup evenly and kept the following beat 1 steady.

quiz.question: The 4& pickup lands...
options: Halfway between beat 4 and the next beat 1
quiz.explanation: It occupies the last eighth-note subdivision of the bar.

lessons.title: Read the low register
lessons.goal: Understand bass clef and the bass guitar's octave convention.
steps: Bass clef lines from bottom are G2 B2 D3 F3 A3; spaces are A2 C3 E3 G3. The two dots of the clef surround the F3 line.
Bass guitar music is normally written one octave above sounding pitch. Open E1 sounds low, but is written E2 on a ledger line below the staff.
Play sounding C2 E2 G2 C3 while the guide shows written C3 E3 G3 C4. Name each pitch before playing it.
Use the ear tool to compare major thirds, fifths and octaves. Hum the interval before moving to the next note on the bass.
lessons.tip: Tab and the fretboard use sounding pitch here. The staff uses the standard written octave for bass guitar.
lessons.pattern: Sounding C2 E2 G2 C3 · written C3 E3 G3 C4
lessons.assessment: I read the pitch guide and explained why written and sounding octaves differ.

quiz.question: A bass guitar's open E1 is normally written as...
quiz.explanation: Bass guitar notation sounds one octave lower than written.

lessons.title: Checkpoint: pocket steps
lessons.goal: Combine roots, fifths and controlled eighth-note pickups.
steps: Use C-F-G-C for four bars, repeated twice, at 60 BPM. Start each bar on its root.
Play root on 1, fifth on 3, and root on 4&. For C use C2/G2; F uses F1/C2; G uses G1/D2.
Keep the note on 4& short so the next root lands clearly. Play along with the original backing and listen for unwanted ringing.
Pass with two uninterrupted eight-bar takes: correct harmony, even subdivisions, and quiet unused strings. Use self-assessment for groove, not the single-note pitch score.
lessons.tip: Being in the pocket means stable time and intentional note length, not simply playing every available beat.
lessons.pattern: Root(1), fifth(3), root(4&) · C F G C ×2
lessons.assessment: I played Pocket Steps twice with clean note lengths and reliable pickups.

quiz.question: What can make an otherwise correct bass line sound untidy?
quiz.explanation: Muting and note length are part of the groove, even when the chosen pitches are correct.

lessons.title: Hear the chord inside the line
lessons.goal: Outline major and minor harmony with thirds and sevenths.
steps: Play C major arpeggio C2-E2-G2-C3. Compare C minor C2-Eb2-G2-C3; lower only the third by one semitone.
For C dominant seventh, use C2-E2-G2-Bb2. Find Bb2 on the G string fret 3. The lowered seventh gives a different pull.
At 45 BPM play one note per beat up and down, keeping the hand shifts quiet. Do not let the first string ring under later notes.
Sing the third before playing it and explain whether the chord is major or minor. Try the ear-training major-third challenge for comparison.
lessons.tip: Chord tones make a line describe harmony even when no full chord is played.
lessons.pattern: C major: C E G C · C minor: C Eb G C · C7: C E G Bb
lessons.assessment: I outlined major, minor and dominant-seventh colours with distinct thirds.

quiz.question: What changes C major into C minor?
quiz.explanation: The minor third is one semitone lower than the major third.

lessons.title: Walk from one chord to the next
lessons.goal: Build a quarter-note walking line with chord tones and approach notes.
steps: At 50 BPM play | C2 E2 G2 E2 | F2 A2 C3 F#2 | G2 B2 D3 B1 | C2 E2 G2 C3 |, one quarter note per beat.
The first note of every bar is its chord root. E leads by a half step to F, F# leads to G, and B1 leads to C2.
Learn each bar separately. D3 is G-string fret 7, F#2 is D-string fret 4, and B1 is A-string fret 2.
Join four bars over C-F-G-C backing. Keep chromatic approaches short and purposeful; listen for the arrival on beat 1 rather than lingering on the approach.
lessons.tip: An approach note can be outside the chord if it resolves clearly. Strong-beat roots keep the harmony grounded.
lessons.pattern: | C E G E | F A C F# | G B D B1 | C E G C |
lessons.assessment: I walked through the progression and resolved each approach on the next root.

quiz.question: Why does F# work just before a G chord?
options: It is the root of C
It approaches G by a semitone
It replaces the need for time
quiz.explanation: The chromatic approach gains meaning by resolving to G on the next strong beat.

lessons.title: Sixteenths without the rush
lessons.goal: Count sixteenth-note subdivisions and keep a sparse groove.
steps: At 40 BPM count 1 e & a 2 e & a 3 e & a 4 e & a. Each beat contains four equally spaced counts.
Mute the strings and tap or pluck once on 1, once on 2&, once on 3, and once on 4a. Count every subdivision, including silence.
Use C2 for the same pattern, alternating fingers only where necessary. Keep the 4a note short before the next beat 1.
Play four clean bars, then change roots C-F-G-C without changing the rhythm. Return to clapping whenever you lose where the numbered beat falls.
lessons.tip: Four notes spread across a bar can be harder than sixteen continuous notes. The rests reveal your internal time.
lessons.assessment: I kept the sparse sixteenth-note groove without rushing the final pickup.

quiz.question: How many equal sixteenth notes fit in one quarter-note beat?
quiz.explanation: The counts number-e-&-a divide one beat into four parts.

lessons.title: A fill that still supports the song
lessons.goal: Place a short fill without losing the next chord's root.
steps: Play three bars of C-F-G roots at 55 BPM. Keep the first two beats of the final C bar simple.
On beats 3, 3&, 4 and 4& play E2 G2 A2 B1, then resolve to C2 on the next beat 1. Learn the fill separately first.
Make a second fill with C major scale notes, ending on a note one step from the next root. Limit it to four eighth notes.
Alternate two cycles with no fill and one cycle with a fill. Listen for whether the fill helps the phrase; reduce notes if the pulse or harmony becomes unclear.
lessons.tip: A fill is a response to a musical space, not a requirement at every bar line.
lessons.pattern: C F G C · final bar fill E G A B1 → C2 on next beat 1
lessons.assessment: I played two different short fills and returned to the root exactly on time.

quiz.question: A useful fill should...
options: Make the next chord arrive late
Lead back to the groove and next root
quiz.explanation: A fill supports the arrangement when it resolves cleanly into the ongoing pulse.

lessons.title: Level test: build the pocket
lessons.goal: Perform a three-section original bass arrangement with consistent time.
steps: Use C-F-G-C for twelve bars at 65 BPM: three four-bar cycles. In cycle 1 play roots on beats 1 and 3.
In cycle 2 use root-fifth patterns with a 4& pickup. In cycle 3 use the quarter-note walking line from the walking lesson.
Add one short fill at the end only if the next C lands on time. Match note length and volume between sections.
Pass with two full twelve-bar takes: steady pulse, deliberate rests, clean muting, correct chord roots, and an unambiguous final C. Explain which section best supports a quiet melody and why.
lessons.tip: These advanced foundations introduce arranging and walking; style-specific time, slap and extended techniques need further focused study.
lessons.pattern: 12 bars: roots / root-fifth / walking · C F G C ×3
lessons.assessment: I performed two complete bass arrangements without losing time or clarity.

quiz.question: When a melody is quiet and spacious, which bass choice may support it best?
quiz.explanation: The best line serves the arrangement, which often means leaving room.
